items.stem: Which term describes the knowledge, skills and qualifications of workers that increase their productivity?
items.answer: Human capital
items.markingKey: Human capital: the knowledge, skills and qualifications of workers that increase their productivity. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “credentialism”? Give one example.
items.answer: The growing demand by employers for qualifications, even for jobs that do not require them. Example: a degree being required for an administrative job.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the growing demand by employers for qualifications, even for jobs that do not require them); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a degree being required for an administrative job. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “knowledge economy” and “skills gap”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Knowledge economy: an economy in which growth depends mainly on information, skills and innovation (e.g. a country focused on software and research). Skills gap: a mismatch between the skills workers have and those employers need (e.g. a shortage of computer programmers).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: The government in Bogotá launches a programme of apprenticeships for 16-year-olds in construction and hospitality, while university places are expanded for top students. Suggest how a Weberian sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Weberian theory: qualifications are used by groups to protect status and access to jobs, so rising requirements reflect credentialism rather than economic need (Collins).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: The government in Kathmandu launches a programme of apprenticeships for 16-year-olds in construction and hospitality, while university places are expanded for top students. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: education develops human capital and allocates people to roles, so it contributes to economic growth; vocational education provides specialist skills for the division of labour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful structured interviews are for studying the link between education and earnings.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; response rates are usually higher than for postal questionnaires because the interviewer is present. Limitations: the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth; the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the link between education and earnings but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “knowledge economy”.
items.answer: An economy in which growth depends mainly on information, skills and innovation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: an economy in which growth depends mainly on information, skills and innovation. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “vocational education” and “human capital”.
items.answer: Vocational education: education and training designed to prepare people for particular jobs or occupations. Human capital: the knowledge, skills and qualifications of workers that increase their productivity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Official earnings data for Bogotá (sample of 600 workers) show the following. Table: median earnings index (all workers = 100) | 2005 | 2025. Degree | 174 | 176. Vocational qualification | 114 | 111. No qualifications | 65 | 61. By how many index points did the figure for Vocational qualification change between 2005 and 2025?
items.answer: -3 index points
items.markingKey: 111 − 114 = -3 index points. [1]

items.stem: Hana is planning a study of young people’s experiences of apprenticeships. Explain one limitation of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for this research.
items.answer: Being studied repeatedly may change participants’ behaviour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of young people’s experiences of apprenticeships. [2]

items.stem: A research team is investigating young people’s experiences of apprenticeships. Explain two limitations of using participant observation for this research.
items.answer: 1. It is time-consuming, costly and may put the researcher at risk. 2. The researcher may become too involved and lose objectivity (“going native”).
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to young people’s experiences of apprenticeships. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes the transfer of public services or assets into the hands of private companies?
items.answer: Privatisation
items.markingKey: Privatisation: the transfer of public services or assets into the hands of private companies. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “silt-shifting”? Give one example.
items.answer: Schools avoiding or offloading pupils with learning difficulties or behaviour problems. Example: excluding pupils likely to lower results.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (schools avoiding or offloading pupils with learning difficulties or behaviour problems); 1 mark for a relevant example such as excluding pupils likely to lower results. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “cream-skimming” and “privatisation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Cream-skimming: schools selecting the most able pupils, who are likely to improve their results (e.g. a popular school admitting high-attaining applicants). Privatisation: the transfer of public services or assets into the hands of private companies (e.g. private companies running state-funded schools).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In Riyadh, the best-performing state schools are surrounded by expensive housing, and their intake is mostly middle-class. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: marketisation and privatisation turn education into a commodity and reproduce class inequality behind a myth of parentocracy (Ball, Gewirtz).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A private company in Doha wins a contract to run testing and management services for a group of state schools. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: education should allocate pupils meritocratically; if choice and competition raise standards they are functional, but unequal access threatens equality of opportunity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A private company in Jakarta wins a contract to run testing and management services for a group of state schools. Compare how Marxist and New Right sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: marketisation and privatisation turn education into a commodity and reproduce class inequality behind a myth of parentocracy (Ball, Gewirtz). New Right: state education is inefficient and does not meet the needs of the economy; competition, parental choice and a market in schools will raise standards (Chubb and Moe), while education should transmit a shared national culture.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful unstructured interviews are for studying how parents from different social classes choose schools.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; rapport between interviewer and interviewee builds trust, so people may reveal more, producing valid data. Limitations: they cannot measure patterns across a large population because only a few people can be interviewed; each interview is unique, so it is hard to repeat and the data is less reliable. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how parents from different social classes choose schools but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying how parents from different social classes choose schools.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how parents from different social classes choose schools but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.answer: Marketisation: introducing competition, choice and business methods into education. Privatisation: the transfer of public services or assets into the hands of private companies.

items.stem: Distinguish between “privatisation” and “cream-skimming”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Privatisation: the transfer of public services or assets into the hands of private companies (e.g. private companies running state-funded schools). Cream-skimming: schools selecting the most able pupils, who are likely to improve their results (e.g. a popular school admitting high-attaining applicants).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Ravi, a sociology student, is designing a project on how parents from different social classes choose schools. Explain one strength of using case studies for this research.
items.answer: They may use several methods, increasing validity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of how parents from different social classes choose schools. [2]

items.stem: Yusuf, a sociology student, is designing a project on how parents from different social classes choose schools. Explain two limitations of using covert participant observation for this research.
items.answer: 1. The researcher may be drawn into illegal or harmful activity and is at risk if discovered. 2. Note-taking is difficult, so data depends on memory and may be inaccurate.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to how parents from different social classes choose schools. [4]

items.stem: Diego, a sociology student, is designing a project on the involvement of private companies in state education. Explain one strength and two limitations of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Strength: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified. Limitations: 1. they cannot tell us how people feel or why they act as they do. 2. definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult.
items.markingKey: For each of three points: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the involvement of private companies in state education. [6]

items.stem: Lucas, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on school intake and league table position in Singapore. The report was based on 120 secondary schools. Table: percentage of pupils eligible for free school meals | 2010 | 2025. Top-third schools | 12% | 8%. Middle-third schools | 25% | 28%. Bottom-third schools | 39% | 41%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Middle-third schools between 2010 and 2025. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that marketisation has increased polarisation between schools.
items.answer: (a) 28 − 25 = +3 percentage points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Middle-third schools, Bottom-third schools; the figure fell for Top-third schools; Bottom-third schools had the highest figure for 2025. Middle-class parents are privileged-skilled choosers (Gewirtz). Qualifications: Differences may reflect housing patterns that existed before marketisation; schools in poorer areas may still improve; free school meal eligibility is only a rough measure of disadvantage. The data also come from official statistics of 120 secondary schools in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 25 and 28; 1 mark for +3 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “global education industry”, and give one example.
items.answer: Multinational businesses that sell education services such as testing, technology and textbooks across countries. Example: a company running exams in over 100 countries.

items.stem: An international company sells the same digital learning platform to schools in Accra and in forty other countries. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: globalisation increases diversity and choice in education but also shows there is no single best system.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A research team is investigating differences in attainment between countries. Explain one strength and one limitation of using official statistics for this study.
items.answer: Strength: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified. Limitation: they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs.
items.markingKey: For each: 1 mark identified; 1 mark explained in the context of differences in attainment between countries. [4]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “global education industry” and “compensatory education”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Global education industry: multinational businesses that sell education services such as testing, technology and textbooks across countries (e.g. a company running exams in over 100 countries). Compensatory education: policies that give extra resources to disadvantaged pupils to make up for deprivation (e.g. extra funding for schools in poor areas).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Colombo wants to research how teachers respond to international league tables. Evaluate the use of field experiments for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they take place in a natural setting, so behaviour is more realistic than in a laboratory; participants usually do not know they are part of an experiment, so they act naturally. Limitations: participants have not given informed consent, which raises ethical issues; the researcher has much less control over variables than in a laboratory. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how teachers respond to international league tables but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) to research differences in attainment between countries.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; comparing the same people at different points avoids the problem of comparing different samples. Limitations: being studied repeatedly may change participants’ behaviour; they are very expensive and results take many years to appear. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying differences in attainment between countries but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Official earnings data for Madrid (sample of 450 workers) show the following. Table: median earnings index (all workers = 100) | 2005 | 2025. Degree | 172 | 162. Vocational qualification | 108 | 110. No qualifications | 72 | 70. (a) Calculate the change, in index points, for Vocational qualification between 2005 and 2025. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that education is a good investment in human capital.
items.answer: (a) 110 − 108 = +2 index points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Vocational qualification; the figure fell for Degree, No qualifications; Degree had the highest figure for 2025. Falling graduate premium may reflect the expansion of higher education. Qualifications: Earnings differences may reflect class background, networks and cultural capital as well as skills; graduate premiums may fall as more people gain degrees; not all graduates get graduate jobs. The data also come from official statistics of 450 workers aged 25-64 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 108 and 110; 1 mark for +2 index points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: The table shows mean scores in an international mathematics test, based on samples of about 800 pupils per country. Table: mean mathematics score (international average about 480) | 2012 | 2022. Country A | 487 | 489. Country B | 513 | 502. Country C | 560 | 558. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Country C between 2012 and 2022. Show your working. (b) Explain one limitation of using official statistics to collect data like these. items.answer: (a) (558 − 560) ÷ 560 × 100 = -0.4%. (b) They are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. Countries with high scores often have high status for teachers and strong cultural emphasis on education. Qualifications: Tests measure a narrow range of skills; samples and translation affect comparability; cultural factors outside school influence results; small score differences may not be significant. The data also come from official statistics of 800 15-year-olds in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (558 − 560) ÷ 560 × 100; 1 mark for -0.4% (accept 2-3 s.f.). items.stem: Official earnings data for Lima (sample of 1200 workers) show the following. Table: median earnings index (all workers = 100) | 2005 | 2025. Degree | 168 | 158. Vocational qualification | 105 | 107. No qualifications | 75 | 72. By how many index points did the figure for Degree change between 2005 and 2025?
items.answer: -10 index points
items.markingKey: 158 − 168 = -10 index points. [1]

items.stem: Yusuf, a sociology student, is designing a project on the link between education and earnings. Explain one strength of using self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the link between education and earnings. [2]

items.stem: Assess how useful official statistics are for studying the link between education and earnings.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are collected regularly, so trends over time and comparisons between groups can be made. Limitations: they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them; definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the link between education and earnings but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes schools selecting the most able pupils, who are likely to improve their results?
items.answer: Cream-skimming
items.markingKey: Cream-skimming: schools selecting the most able pupils, who are likely to improve their results. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “silt-shifting”?
items.answer: Schools avoiding or offloading pupils with learning difficulties or behaviour problems.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: schools avoiding or offloading pupils with learning difficulties or behaviour problems. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Parentocracy means all parents have equal power to choose schools.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Ball and Gewirtz argue choice favours middle-class parents with more capital; parentocracy is a myth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which marketisation may benefit middle-class pupils more than working-class pupils.
items.answer: Middle-class parents have economic capital (selection by mortgage, transport, tutoring); cultural capital to understand admissions; social capital to get information; schools cream-skim desirable pupils.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of school intake and league table position (120 secondary schools, Manila). Table: percentage of pupils eligible for free school meals | 2010 | 2025. Top-third schools | 13% | 11%. Middle-third schools | 18% | 18%. Bottom-third schools | 34% | 36%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Top-third schools change between 2010 and 2025?
items.answer: -2 percentage points
items.markingKey: 11 − 13 = -2 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Samuel is planning a study of the involvement of private companies in state education. Explain one limitation of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: They cannot tell us how people feel or why they act as they do.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the involvement of private companies in state education. [2]

items.stem: A private company in Madrid wins a contract to run testing and management services for a group of state schools. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: marketisation and privatisation turn education into a commodity and reproduce class inequality behind a myth of parentocracy (Ball, Gewirtz).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Omar, a sociology student, is designing a project on how parents from different social classes choose schools. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how parents from different social classes choose schools but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of school intake and league table position (60 secondary schools, Seoul). Table: percentage of pupils eligible for free school meals | 2010 | 2025. Top-third schools | 13% | 11%. Middle-third schools | 18% | 18%. Bottom-third schools | 38% | 45%. (a) Calculate the gap between Middle-third schools and Top-third schools in 2010 and in 2025, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Explain one limitation of using official statistics to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that marketisation has increased polarisation between schools.
items.answer: (a) 2010: 5 percentage points; 2025: 7 percentage points; the gap widened. (b) They show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Bottom-third schools; the figure fell for Top-third schools; Bottom-third schools had the highest figure for 2025. Cream-skimming by popular schools concentrates disadvantaged pupils in less popular schools (Bartlett). Qualifications: Differences may reflect housing patterns that existed before marketisation; schools in poorer areas may still improve; free school meal eligibility is only a rough measure of disadvantage. The data also come from official statistics of 60 secondary schools in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (5 and 7); 1 mark for “widened”. [3] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment, which tests 15-year-olds in reading, mathematics and science in many countries?
items.answer: PISA
items.markingKey: PISA: the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment, which tests 15-year-olds in reading, mathematics and science in many countries. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which globalisation has influenced education policy.
items.answer: International league tables (PISA) create pressure to raise standards; policy borrowing between countries; global education businesses; emphasis on skills for a global knowledge economy; international qualifications and student migration.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: An international company sells the same digital learning platform to schools in Hanoi and in forty other countries. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: globalisation increases diversity and choice in education but also shows there is no single best system.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A sociologist in Nairobi wants to research how teachers respond to international league tables. Explain two strengths of using field experiments for this research.
items.answer: 1. One variable can be altered (for example the name on a job application) to test its effect. 2. They take place in a natural setting, so behaviour is more realistic than in a laboratory.
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to how teachers respond to international league tables. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying how teachers respond to international league tables.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can explain unclear questions, so fewer answers are spoiled; response rates are usually higher than for postal questionnaires because the interviewer is present. Limitations: the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth; they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how teachers respond to international league tables but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]
